articles.title: Cellular Recycling — The Science of Autophagy and the Nobel Prize That Unlocked It
articles.subtitle: Inside every living cell, a remarkable survival process is quietly at work — breaking down waste, recycling damaged components, and keeping your body running. This is autophagy, and understanding it could change how you think about health, aging, and fasting.
articles.author: Sasha Gaye Hemmings | LWS Media Network
articles.coverImageCaption: Cellular Recycling — The Science of Autophagy. Photo: LWS Media Network
articles.excerpt: Inside every living cell, a remarkable survival process is quietly at work — breaking down waste, recycling damaged components, and keeping your body running. This is the science of autophagy, the Nobel Prize discovery that changed medicine forever.

body.text: The word autophagy originates from the Greek words auto, meaning self, and phagy, meaning eating. It describes a critical, survival-driven physiological process where cells degrade and recycle their own internal components to generate energy and maintain structural health. Far from being a destructive act, this self-eating function serves as the body's ultimate internal house-cleaning system — and understanding it is transforming how scientists and doctors think about disease, aging, and the human body.
How Autophagy Works

Under normal conditions, cells consistently accumulate waste — misfolded proteins, damaged metabolic machinery, and invading pathogens. If left unmanaged, this cellular garbage triggers inflammation and accelerates aging. Autophagy functions as an automated cleanup crew through a specific multi-step sequence that is elegant in its precision.

It begins with isolation membrane formation — the cell identifies waste material and constructs a temporary, double-layered membrane around it. This membrane closes completely, sealing the waste inside a specialized storage vesicle called an autophagosome. The autophagosome then travels through the cell and fuses with a lysosome — an organelle packed with acidic, digestive enzymes. Those enzymes break the trapped waste down into its foundational building blocks, such as raw amino acids and fatty acids. The cell then pumps these renewed nutrients back into its cytoplasm to construct pristine cellular parts or to fuel survival.
Autophagy is not destruction — it is transformation. The cell does not simply throw away its waste. It converts that waste into fuel and uses it to build something better.
body.cite: Sasha Gaye Hemmings, LWS Media Network

body.text: Starvation and the Self-Eating Mechanism

When a person consumes food regularly, the hormone insulin and a nutrient-sensing protein complex called mTOR remain active, signalling cells to grow and pause the recycling process. But when food is entirely absent — such as during intentional fasting or starvation — nutrient levels drop sharply. The body responds by deactivating mTOR and aggressively triggering autophagy.

Instead of shutting down from a lack of external calories, the cell systematically prioritises and consumes its most damaged, non-essential internal elements first. It selectively dismantles old proteins and failing mitochondria to keep vital organs supplied with energy. In short, the body intentionally burns its internal trash to keep its metabolic engine running safely. This is why fasting has been studied so intensively in recent years — it is not merely about calorie restriction. It is about triggering one of the body's most powerful biological maintenance systems.
Yoshinori Ohsumi and the 2016 Nobel Prize

While scientists first observed the physical structures of autophagy in the 1960s using early electron microscopes, the actual genetic commands driving the process remained completely unknown for three decades. The mechanism existed — but nobody knew how it was controlled at the molecular level.

In the early 1990s, Japanese cell biologist Dr. Yoshinori Ohsumi, working at the Tokyo Institute of Technology, set out to solve this puzzle using ordinary baker's yeast. Yeast cells are incredibly small and their internal structures are difficult to distinguish under a standard lens. Dr. Ohsumi engineered a specialised strain of yeast that lacked the digestive enzymes required to break down waste. When he intentionally starved these engineered cells, an astonishing phenomenon occurred — tiny autophagic vesicles rapidly filled up the yeast's central vacuole, unable to degrade. Because the process stopped mid-way, the vesicles accumulated, making them plainly visible under a microscope for the first time.

Using this visual breakthrough, Ohsumi exposed the yeast to chemicals that caused random genetic mutations. He observed which mutated cells failed to accumulate these vesicles when starved. Through this screening method, he successfully identified 15 essential genes — originally named APG genes, now classified as ATG genes — that directly command autophagy in living organisms. He subsequently proved that human cells utilise these exact same genetic pathways to recycle waste.

For these foundational discoveries, the Karolinska Institutet awarded Dr. Yoshinori Ohsumi the 2016 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. It was a recognition long overdue for work that had quietly been reshaping the foundations of cellular biology for over two decades.
Ohsumi did not set out to win a Nobel Prize. He set out to understand how a yeast cell survives starvation. What he found changed our understanding of every living organism on earth — including us.
body.cite: Sasha Gaye Hemmings, LWS Media Network

body.text: Medical and Clinical Implications

Ohsumi's work completely revolutionised modern medicine by revealing that disruptions in autophagy are directly tied to severe human illnesses. In neurodegenerative diseases like Alzheimer's and Parkinson's, toxic protein aggregates clog brain cells and destroy them over time. Boosting autophagy may help clear these plaques — opening a potential therapeutic pathway that did not exist before Ohsumi's discoveries.

In oncology, autophagy plays a complex dual role. In early stages, it prevents tumors by destroying mutated cells before they can proliferate. In advanced stages, however, aggressive cancer cells can hijack autophagy to survive chemotherapy — a discovery that is reshaping how oncologists think about treatment resistance. Autophagy also directly targets and eliminates invading cellular viruses and intracellular bacteria, making it a critical component of immune defence.

Perhaps most significantly for the long term, researchers have found that autophagic efficiency naturally declines as humans age. The cellular cleaning system slows down. Waste accumulates. Dysfunction follows. This has made exploring lifestyle factors like intermittent fasting and caloric restriction a major focus for clinical anti-aging research — with implications that reach far beyond nutrition into the fundamental science of how long and how well we live.
What Comes Next

Understanding autophagy at the scientific level is only the beginning. The more practical question — and the one that affects how you live every day — is how to activate and support this process through diet, exercise, and lifestyle choices. In Part 2 of this series, we will explore exactly that: how intermittent fasting, specific exercise protocols, and dietary compounds known as autophagy mimetics can switch on your body's cellular recycling system and what the science actually says about each one.
The body already knows how to heal itself at the cellular level. The science of autophagy is teaching us how to get out of its way.

articles.title: The Cosmic Exorcist — Why a Prominent Washington Priest Was Fired Over His UFO Demon Rant
articles.subtitle: Cardinal Robert McElroy removed Monsignor Stephen Rossetti as the Archdiocese of Washington's chief exorcist after a viral video claimed UFO sightings are demonic manifestations designed to manipulate humanity.
articles.author: Sasha Gaye Hemmings | LWS Media Network
articles.coverImageCaption: Monsignor Stephen Rossetti, former chief exorcist of the Archdiocese of Washington. Photo: The New York Times
articles.excerpt: A prominent Washington priest, licensed psychologist, and chief exorcist went viral after claiming UFO sightings are demonic manifestations. Cardinal Robert McElroy responded swiftly — firing him and severing all ties with his ministry organization.

body.text: The escalating conversation around Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena has breached the walls of the Vatican and triggered an unprecedented theological showdown in the nation's capital. At the center of it is a prominent priest, a viral video, and a question that sits at the intersection of faith, science, and the unknown — what exactly are UFOs?
The Firing

Cardinal Robert McElroy, the Archbishop of Washington, announced the immediate removal of Monsignor Stephen Rossetti from his long-standing role as the Archdiocese of Washington's chief exorcist. The dismissal was swift and decisive. Alongside Rossetti's personal termination, the Archdiocese completely severed its affiliation with the St. Michael Center for Spiritual Renewal — a prominent Washington-based non-profit organization headed by the priest that specialised in deliverance ministries and treating psychologically troubled clergy.

Rossetti is not an obscure figure. He is a licensed psychologist, a published author, and one of the most high-profile exorcists in the United States. He had served in his role for years and built a significant public platform. His removal sent shockwaves through both the Catholic community and the broader conversation around UAP disclosure that has been growing in intensity since the US government began releasing classified materials.
The Video That Started It All

The controversy ignited on May 29, 2026, when Rossetti published a video to his Facebook and Instagram pages — where he commands a combined following of over 148,000 users. Addressing the recent influx of government UAP declassifications, Rossetti drew on his two decades of exorcism experience to offer an interpretation that stopped many people cold.

In the video, Rossetti warned that the physics-defying maneuvers reported in UAP sightings resemble the spiritual deception he encounters in his exorcism work. He suggested that demons — which he described as invisible entities — seek to influence humanity, and expressed his personal belief that many UFO sightings are in fact demonic manifestations rather than extraterrestrial visitors. The video went viral almost immediately, generating fierce debate across religious, scientific, and UAP research communities.

When a credentialed psychologist and senior Catholic priest tells 148,000 followers that UFOs are demons — and gets fired for it by his own archdiocese — that is a story that demands serious attention.
body.cite: Sasha Gaye Hemmings, LWS Media Network

body.text: Why the Church Acted So Quickly

The speed of the Archdiocese's response is itself telling. Cardinal McElroy did not issue a statement distancing the Church from Rossetti's views or ask him to clarify his position. He removed him entirely and cut institutional ties with his ministry organisation in a single decisive move. That kind of response suggests the Church felt the claims were not merely theologically controversial — but potentially damaging to its credibility and its relationship with the broader public conversation around UAP disclosure.

The Catholic Church has historically navigated the question of extraterrestrial life with more nuance than many people expect. Vatican astronomers have spoken openly about the possibility of life on other planets without theological contradiction. Rossetti's framing — presenting UAPs specifically as demonic deception — appears to have crossed a line that the institutional Church was not willing to publicly endorse.
The Bigger Picture — UAPs, Faith, and the Unknown

This story matters beyond the specific circumstances of one priest's firing. It sits at the collision point of several massive conversations happening simultaneously — the US government's ongoing UAP disclosure process, the question of how religious institutions respond to phenomena that challenge traditional frameworks, and the very human tendency to interpret the unknown through the lens of whatever belief system we already hold.

Whether UAPs represent advanced technology, natural phenomena, extraterrestrial intelligence, or something else entirely remains genuinely unresolved. The science is actively evolving. What is clear is that the conversation is no longer fringe — it is happening in congressional hearings, military briefings, and now apparently in the offices of Catholic cardinals. When a topic reaches that many rooms simultaneously, it deserves serious, honest coverage.

Monsignor Rossetti offered his interpretation through the framework of his faith and his professional experience as an exorcist. His archdiocese disagreed strongly enough to end his career in that role. The debate about what is actually in our skies — and what it means — is far from over.

Whether you believe in demons, extraterrestrials, or neither — the fact that this conversation is now happening at the highest levels of government and religion tells you something important. Pay attention.

articles.title: The Iran War Powers Vote — Can Congress Stop President Trump?
articles.subtitle: The US House voted 215 to 208 to demand an end to military action against Iran. But between a concurrent resolution, a veto, and a two-thirds override threshold, the White House still holds the upper hand.
articles.author: Sasha Gaye Hemmings | LWS Media Network
articles.coverImageCaption: The US House of Representatives votes to challenge President Trump's war powers over Iran. Photo: LWS Media Network
articles.excerpt: The US House voted 215 to 208 to demand an end to military action against Iran — the sharpest challenge yet to President Trump's wartime powers. But can Congress actually force the President to stop a war? Here is the plain-language breakdown.

body.text: In a dramatic confrontation over executive authority, the US House of Representatives voted 215 to 208 to demand an end to ongoing military action against Iran. The high-stakes vote marks the sharpest challenge yet to President Donald Trump's wartime powers since conflict erupted four months ago. But it has left many Americans asking a critical question: can Congress actually force the President to stop a war?
What Just Happened in the House?

The House passed a War Powers resolution — H.Con.Res. 86 — declaring that the Trump administration has exceeded its constitutional authority. Under the War Powers Act of 1973, a president must secure explicit congressional approval to sustain military operations past a 60 to 90 day window. Because the conflict has entered its fourth month without a formal declaration of war, lawmakers moved to assert their constitutional right to control when the nation goes to war.

The vote was notable for rare bipartisan friction. Four Republicans — Representatives Brian Fitzpatrick, Thomas Massie, Tom Barrett, and Warren Davidson — crossed party lines to join Democrats in voting to halt the hostilities. That fracture within the President's own party is perhaps the most politically significant detail in this story. When members of your own party start breaking ranks on a war, the political ground is shifting.
Can President Trump Veto the Vote?

The short answer is no — but there is a major legal catch. Because the House passed this measure as a concurrent resolution, it is technically exempt from a presidential veto. It never travels to the President's desk for a signature. However, by bypassing the President, a concurrent resolution loses its legal teeth. It does not carry the full enforcement power of federal law. What it does carry is significant political weight — a formal, public declaration that the President is operating without the consent of the legislature.

If Congress wants to make the mandate legally binding, they must pass it as a joint resolution. But doing so triggers a constitutional mechanism that plays directly into the President's hands — the veto power. And that is where the math becomes very uncomfortable for war opponents.
The Math of the Presidential Veto

If a joint resolution reaches the White House, President Trump would almost certainly veto it. To override that veto and force the resolution into law, Congress would need a two-thirds absolute majority in both chambers. Here is the reality of the numbers:

In the House, an override requires 290 votes. The current resolution only passed with 215. Congress is short by 75 votes. In the Senate, an override requires 67 votes. Republicans currently hold a slim majority — meaning dozens of the President's closest political allies would have to rebel against him to reach that number. The arithmetic is clear. Opponents of the war do not have the numbers to override a veto. President Trump retains ultimate control over military strategy.

A concurrent resolution is a powerful political statement. But political statements do not ground aircraft or withdraw troops. The hard truth is that Congress has expressed its will — and for now, the President does not have to listen.
body.cite: Sasha Gaye Hemmings, LWS Media Network

body.text: Where Does the Conflict Go From Here?

For now, the war will continue. The Trump administration has dismissed the House vote as meaningless and unpatriotic, arguing that a brief April ceasefire meant hostilities technically ceased — a claim Congress fiercely rejects following recent heavy flare-ups in regional fighting. The legal debate over what constitutes a continuation of conflict versus a new engagement is itself a political battleground.

The political battle now moves to the US Senate. While the Senate advanced a parallel measure in a narrow 50 to 47 procedural vote last month, final passage faces a steep uphill climb. The numbers simply do not favour those seeking to legally constrain the President's military authority.
Why This Vote Still Matters

While the House vote may not physically ground aircraft or withdraw troops today, it sends a message that cannot be ignored. The political consensus supporting the war with Iran is fracturing. Four Republicans breaking ranks is not just a statistic — it is a signal. When a president loses members of his own party on a war vote, the political calculus of the conflict begins to shift in ways that go beyond any single legislative outcome.

History has shown that wars sustained without broad political support become progressively harder to maintain — not just militarily, but politically and economically. The War Powers Act itself was born out of exactly that kind of fracture during the Vietnam era. Congress is not stopping this war today. But it is putting the White House on notice that the clock is running.
This is the story behind the vote. Not just what happened — but what it means. Stay informed, stay aware, and keep asking the questions that the headlines do not always answer.

articles.title: Earth Before Us — The Lost World of Extinction, Evolution, Climate Change, and Human Origins
articles.subtitle: More than 99 percent of all species that have ever lived are now extinct. The Earth we know today is not the Earth that has always existed — and understanding what came before us changes everything about how we see ourselves.
articles.author: Sasha Gaye Hemmings | LWS Media Network
articles.coverImageCaption: Earth Before Us — billions of years of life, extinction, and survival. Photo: LWS Media Network
articles.excerpt: More than 99 percent of all species that have ever lived are now extinct. The Earth we know today is the product of repeated cycles of creation and destruction spanning 4.5 billion years — and understanding that lost world changes everything about how we see ourselves.

body.text: When most people think about Earth's history, they imagine dinosaurs roaming ancient forests millions of years ago. Yet dinosaurs represent only a small chapter in a story spanning more than 4.5 billion years. The Earth we know today is not the Earth that has always existed. Scientists estimate that more than 99 percent of all species that have ever lived are now extinct. Every tree, bird, insect, mammal, and human alive today exists as part of a tiny surviving fraction of life's vast history.

The modern world is the product of repeated cycles of creation and destruction. Entire ecosystems have appeared and vanished. Oceans have advanced and retreated. Continents have collided and broken apart. Massive volcanic eruptions have altered the atmosphere. Asteroid impacts have reshaped evolution. Species have risen to dominance and disappeared forever. To understand humanity's place in nature, we must first understand the ancient world that existed long before us.
A Planet Born From Fire

Earth formed approximately 4.54 billion years ago from a swirling cloud of dust and gas surrounding the young Sun. The early Earth was a hostile place. Molten rock covered much of the surface. Asteroids and comets bombarded the planet regularly. Volcanoes released enormous quantities of gases into the atmosphere. There were no forests, no animals, no oceans filled with fish, no oxygen-rich atmosphere. The world was largely unrecognizable.

Over millions of years, the planet gradually cooled. Water vapor condensed into liquid water, forming Earth's first oceans. These oceans became the cradle of life. Scientists believe the earliest life emerged more than 3.5 billion years ago. These first organisms were microscopic and incredibly simple compared with modern life. Yet these tiny organisms would eventually transform the entire planet.
The Great Oxygen Revolution

For nearly half of Earth's history, there was little free oxygen in the atmosphere. Then a remarkable group of microorganisms known as cyanobacteria began using sunlight to produce energy through photosynthesis. As a byproduct, they released oxygen. Over hundreds of millions of years, oxygen accumulated in the atmosphere, triggering what scientists call the Great Oxygenation Event.

This event changed everything. Many ancient organisms that could not tolerate oxygen disappeared. At the same time, oxygen made more complex forms of life possible. Without this transformation, animals, plants, and eventually humans could never have evolved. A microscopic organism breathing out a gas transformed the trajectory of life on Earth forever.
Life Begins in the Ocean

One of the most important facts in biology is that all known vertebrate life traces its ancestry to aquatic organisms. Long before forests covered continents, life flourished in the seas. Ancient oceans contained trilobites, primitive fish, jellyfish-like organisms, early arthropods, and countless extinct species that left no descendants. For hundreds of millions of years, the oceans were the center of biological innovation.

The earliest vertebrates resembled simple fish. Over time, evolution produced more advanced forms with jaws, stronger skeletons, and improved mobility. These developments laid the foundation for one of the greatest transitions in Earth's history. Life would eventually leave the water.
When Fish Learned to Walk

Around 375 million years ago, certain fish began developing characteristics that would allow them to survive in shallow wetlands. These were not fish suddenly transforming into amphibians in a single generation. Rather, small changes accumulated over millions of years — stronger fins, more robust bones, primitive lungs, improved neck mobility, and a greater ability to support their own weight.

One famous transitional fossil, Tiktaalik, possessed features of both fish and land animals. It had scales and fins but also bones resembling those found in the limbs of terrestrial vertebrates. Eventually these evolutionary experiments produced the first tetrapods — four-limbed vertebrates capable of moving onto land. Every amphibian, reptile, bird, and mammal alive today descends from these pioneering creatures. Including us. The bones in a human arm share a remarkably similar structural pattern with the fins of ancient fish ancestors. The evidence of our aquatic origins remains embedded within our own anatomy.
The Age of Giant Forests

As plants colonized land, vast forests emerged. During the Carboniferous Period, approximately 359 to 299 million years ago, immense swamp forests stretched across large portions of the planet. These forests were unlike anything alive today. Towering club mosses reached heights comparable to modern trees. Massive ferns dominated landscapes. Giant insects thrived in oxygen-rich air. Dragonflies grew wingspans exceeding two feet. Millipede-like creatures reached lengths greater than six feet.

Many of these forests would eventually become the coal deposits modern societies use for energy. Every piece of coal is essentially compressed ancient plant matter from ecosystems that disappeared hundreds of millions of years ago. When we burn coal, we are releasing carbon that was locked away by forests that no living human could have imagined.
The Age of Endless Rain and Climate Chaos

Earth's climate has never been stable. Throughout geological history, the planet experienced dramatic swings between extremes. One particularly significant event occurred during the Carnian Pluvial Episode roughly 234 million years ago. Scientists believe massive volcanic eruptions released enormous quantities of carbon dioxide into the atmosphere. Global temperatures changed. Weather patterns shifted. Rainfall increased dramatically across large regions of the world.

For perhaps millions of years, unusually wet conditions transformed ecosystems. Species adapted or disappeared. New evolutionary opportunities emerged. Geological evidence indicates that certain regions experienced prolonged periods of intense rainfall unlike anything humans have witnessed in recorded history. Earth's deep past is a reminder that climate has always been one of the most powerful forces capable of reshaping life — long before human industry ever entered the picture.

Climate change is not a modern invention. It is one of the oldest forces on this planet. What is modern is the speed at which we are driving it — and the consequences we are only beginning to understand.
body.cite: Sasha Gaye Hemmings, LWS Media Network

body.text: The Rise and Reign of the Dinosaurs

Following earlier extinction events, dinosaurs emerged and eventually became the dominant land animals. For approximately 165 million years, dinosaurs occupied nearly every terrestrial environment. Some were small hunters. Others were feathered. Some grew larger than modern buildings. Contrary to popular belief, dinosaurs were not evolutionary failures. They were among the most successful groups of animals ever to exist — ruling the planet for a period of time so vast it makes all of human history look like a brief footnote.

The world of the dinosaurs included vast forests, giant predators, flying reptiles, early mammals, and diverse ecosystems spanning the globe. For millions of years, they appeared unstoppable. Then catastrophe struck.
The Asteroid That Changed Everything

Approximately 66 million years ago, a large asteroid struck near what is now Mexico. The impact released energy equivalent to billions of nuclear bombs. Wildfires spread. Dust filled the atmosphere. Sunlight decreased. Food chains collapsed. The extinction event eliminated approximately 75 percent of Earth's species. Non-avian dinosaurs vanished from the planet entirely.

Yet some descendants survived. Today, every bird on Earth is considered a living dinosaur. The pigeons in city parks and the eagles soaring overhead are distant descendants of creatures that survived one of the worst disasters in planetary history. Extinction is devastating — but survival is possible even from the edge of annihilation.
The Truth About Extinction — More Than 99 Percent Are Gone

Perhaps the most astonishing fact in paleontology is that virtually every species that has ever existed is now extinct. The Earth today contains only a tiny fraction of life's historical diversity. Species disappear for many reasons — environmental change, competition, disease, climate shifts, habitat loss, and catastrophic events. Extinction is not the exception. It is the rule. The history of life is largely a history of disappearance.

The species alive today represent survivors of countless biological experiments conducted over billions of years. We are not the intended outcome of evolution. We are simply the ones who made it this far — so far.
The Rise of Mammals and the Human Story

After the dinosaur extinction, mammals expanded into newly available ecological niches. Over millions of years, mammals evolved into numerous forms. Some returned to the oceans and became whales. Others took to the air as bats. Primates eventually emerged among the forests. These primates would produce one lineage unlike any before it — the human lineage.

Genetics, archaeology, and fossil evidence overwhelmingly support the conclusion that modern humans originated in Africa. Homo sapiens evolved approximately 300,000 years ago. Africa contains the deepest and most diverse branches of human genetic variation — precisely what scientists expect from the region where our species first evolved. Every living human ultimately traces ancestry back to African populations. This is not a theory. It is one of the strongest conclusions in modern science.
The Great Human Migration

Around 60,000 to 70,000 years ago, groups of humans began expanding beyond Africa. Over thousands of years, populations spread into the Middle East, Europe, Asia, Australia, Siberia, and eventually the Americas. These journeys required remarkable adaptability. Humans survived deserts, mountains, forests, ice ages, and environments entirely unlike anything their ancestors had known. The migration transformed a regional African species into a global one.

Human skin pigmentation evolved as part of this journey — primarily in response to ultraviolet radiation. Near the equator, darker skin containing more melanin helped protect against harmful ultraviolet radiation. As populations moved into regions with lower sunlight levels, lighter skin gradually evolved in many groups because it improved vitamin D production. This process occurred over thousands of generations. All humans remain extraordinarily similar genetically. The visible differences between populations represent only a tiny fraction of our genetic makeup. Modern science has demonstrated clearly that race is a social concept far more than a biological one. Humanity remains one species with a shared origin.
We Are the Survivors of Deep Time

The story of Earth is not merely the story of dinosaurs or humans. It is the story of survival. Life emerged from ancient oceans. Fish became land animals. Forests rose and vanished. Rain-soaked worlds transformed ecosystems. Mass extinctions erased most species that ever existed. Dinosaurs ruled the Earth and disappeared. Humans emerged in Africa and spread across the globe.

Today we stand as products of billions of years of evolutionary history. Every breath we take, every bone in our body, and every cell in our DNA carries echoes of ancient oceans, vanished forests, extinct species, and ancestral journeys across continents. We are not separate from Earth's history. We are one of its most recent chapters — and the choices we make right now will determine what the next chapter looks like.
We did not inherit this planet from our ancestors. We borrowed it from our children. And the story of what came before us should make us far more careful about what we leave behind.

articles.title: UNDERREPORTED: The Rohingya Forgotten Again — and Somalia's Silent Famine Warning
articles.subtitle: Two crises. Two regions. One devastating pattern — the world keeps cutting funding for the people who need it most, and the cameras keep looking away.
articles.author: Sasha Gaye Hemmings | LWS Media Network
articles.coverImageCaption: Underreported: Weh Dem Nuh Seh — stories the world chooses not to tell. Photo: LWS Media Network
articles.excerpt: More than 1.2 million Rohingya refugees remain trapped in Bangladesh as international funding dries up. In Somalia, 6 million people face severe food insecurity and the famine warning signs are already here. Two crises, one pattern — the world is not paying attention.

body.text: Welcome to Underreported: Weh Dem Nuh Seh — where global crises do not fade into silence just because the news cycle moved on. Today we are covering two stories that have been eclipsed by louder headlines but are too critical to ignore. One is about a refugee population the world decided was no longer worth covering. The other is about a famine that is building quietly — right now — while the window to prevent it narrows by the day.
The Rohingya Crisis — The Funding Disappeared, The People Did Not

Nearly nine years have passed since hundreds of thousands of Rohingya fled Myanmar in one of the most documented mass displacements of the 21st century. The images were everywhere. The international outcry was loud. And then — as it always does — the news cycle moved on. But the crisis did not.

More than 1.2 million Rohingya refugees remain in overcrowded camps in Bangladesh. They did not go home. They were not resettled. They are still there — in conditions that have not improved and in many ways have worsened. Since 2024, new violence in Myanmar has forced another 150,000 people to flee, adding further strain to a system that was already stretched beyond its limits.

And now the international funding that keeps those camps functioning is shrinking. Food assistance, healthcare, education, shelter programs — all facing cuts. Not because the need is not there. The need is as acute as it has ever been. The cuts are happening because the world has quietly decided this is an old story. Women, children, and the elderly bear the worst of it. And as conditions deteriorate, more refugees are attempting dangerous sea journeys to find a way out — with hundreds reported dead or missing in the process.

When a humanitarian crisis becomes old news, the suffering does not become old too. It compounds. Every year of inaction is another year of lives suspended in limbo with no path home and no sustainable future.
body.cite: Sasha Gaye Hemmings, LWS Media Network

body.text: This is what chronic underfunding looks like in practice. Refugee camps that depend almost entirely on international support are being told to do more with less — while the people inside them have no alternatives, no power, and no platform loud enough to force the world to listen again. The Rohingya crisis did not end. The attention did. And that distinction is costing lives.
Somalia — A Famine Warning Nobody Is Talking About

On the other side of the world, another quiet emergency is building. UN agencies are warning that roughly 6 million people in Somalia face severe food insecurity this year. Nearly 1.9 million children are suffering from acute malnutrition. Almost half a million of those children face severe acute malnutrition — the most dangerous form, the one that kills.

This did not happen overnight. Years of drought, economic shocks, conflict, and displacement have stripped communities of their ability to absorb crisis after crisis. There is no buffer left. When the rains fail — and experts warn they may — and when aid does not arrive at the scale required, the trajectory from food insecurity to famine is not a distant possibility. It is a predictable outcome.

Humanitarian funding shortages are already limiting the ability of aid agencies to respond. The organisations on the ground are not being quiet about this — they are raising the alarm as loudly as they can. But a famine warning in Somalia does not trend. It does not generate the same outrage as other stories. And so the window to prevent a larger catastrophe keeps closing, quietly, while the world looks elsewhere.

Hunger emergencies do not arrive suddenly. They build slowly, one missed meal, one failed harvest, one defunded programme at a time — until intervention becomes far more difficult, far more expensive, and for some, too late.
body.cite: Sasha Gaye Hemmings, LWS Media Network

body.text: The Pattern Nobody Wants to Name

Bangladesh and Somalia are thousands of miles apart. The Rohingya crisis and Somalia's food emergency have different histories, different causes, and different dynamics. But they reveal the same pattern — a growing gap between humanitarian need and humanitarian funding, in a world that has decided certain suffering is simply less urgent than other suffering.

Refugees in Bangladesh, hungry families in Somalia, vulnerable communities across the African continent — these are people whose lives are being shaped not only by conflict and climate shocks but by whether the international community chooses to keep paying attention. And right now, it is choosing not to.

That choice has consequences. Real, measurable, human consequences. The children going to sleep malnourished in Mogadishu tonight are not an abstraction. The families in Cox's Bazar who have been waiting nine years for a future that has not come are not statistics. They are people. And their stories deserve to be told — not once, loudly, and then forgotten — but consistently, persistently, and with the same urgency that the world reserves for crises closer to home.
We call them underreported. But you need to know. Bring these stories to light — and pass them on.

body.text: Good morning, and welcome to Weh Yuh Seh Views. I am your host, Sasha — bringing you global news you can trust in just a few minutes. Here are today's headlines for June 3, 2026.

articles.title: From Portmore to the Field — The Journey of Alex Palmer
articles.subtitle: Born in Jamaica, raised by a village of love, and shaped by the game he gave everything to — Alex Palmer's story is about migration, sacrifice, and what it means to bloom where you are planted.
articles.author: LWS Media Network
articles.coverImageCaption: Alex Palmer — South Fork Bulldogs Varsity Football, #21 Cornerback. Photo provided courtesy of family.
articles.excerpt: Born in Portmore, St. Catherine, Jamaica and raised by a village of family love — Alex Palmer wore jersey #21 for the South Fork Bulldogs, played varsity football from 2021 to 2024, and is now 20 years old with college on the horizon and a story worth knowing.

body.text: There is a particular kind of strength that comes from being uprooted young. From leaving everything familiar — the sounds, the streets, the faces — and being planted somewhere entirely new, expected to grow. Alex Palmer knows that strength intimately. He was born in Portmore, St. Catherine, Jamaica, and when he was in grade seven his world changed. He migrated to Florida with his mother, leaving behind the island that shaped his earliest years and stepping into a new chapter that would define the rest of them.
He is twenty years old at the time of this article. And already his story is one worth telling.
Portmore to Florida — A Journey Built on Family

Portmore is a municipality in St. Catherine, Jamaica — a place known for its tight communities, its culture, and the kind of upbringing that instils values early. Alex grew up there with both parents before migration changed the geography of his life. When he and his mother made the move to Florida, they did not arrive alone in the way that word implies. They arrived into the arms of family.

His grandmother was the anchor. She was the one who filed for Alex and his mother, who helped make the move possible, and who was present in the years that followed — helping to raise him while his mother worked hard to build a stable life. His grandmother did not just open a door for them. She stood at that door and held it open with her whole body, for as long as it took.

She passed away after Alex finished high school. The timing carries its own quiet weight — she stayed long enough to see him through. Long enough to see what she helped build. That is not a small thing. That is a life well lived and a love that deserves to be remembered.
Behind every young person who makes it, there is almost always someone who quietly made it possible. For Alex, that person was his grandmother.
body.cite: LWS Media Network

body.text: The Bulldogs — Finding a Home on the Field

Alex completed his high school years at South Fork High School in Stuart, Florida — home of the Bulldogs. For a young man navigating a new country, a new school, and a new culture, sport has a way of cutting through all of that. It gives you a team. It gives you a role. It gives you a reason to show up every day with a clear purpose.

Alex found that in football. He joined the South Fork Bulldogs football program in 2021 and wore jersey number 21 as a cornerback on the varsity team. He remained on the roster through to his graduation in 2024 — three years of showing up, putting in the work, and representing his school and his community on that field.

In the 2023-24 season Alex recorded tackles on the varsity level — including a standout moment in the Bulldogs win over Port St. Lucie on October 20, 2023, where South Fork won 36-27 and Alex contributed with solo tackles on the defensive side. For a cornerback, defence is identity. It is the position of the athlete who stands between the opposition and the end zone — alert, disciplined, and unafraid of contact.

body.caption: Alex Palmer at prom — a milestone moment captured. Photo provided courtesy of family.

body.text: The Village That Raised Him

Alex is the only child of his mother — a woman who has given everything to make life smooth for her son. The kind of mother who carries the weight of a family on her shoulders without making it look like a burden, because her child's opportunities are worth every sacrifice. Alex has felt that sacrifice and he carries it with him.

But the love around him has never been limited to one person. Alex has grown up supported by extended family from both his mother's side and his father's side — a web of connection that stretches across Florida and back to Jamaica. He is also the older brother of Samara Palmer. Samara — at nine years old a published author and the inspiration behind a global learning platform — is the kind of little sister who makes a big brother proud simply by existing with that much light.

The African proverb says it takes a village to raise a child. Alex Palmer is the living evidence of what a village looks like when it shows up fully — a grandmother who filed the papers, a mother who never stopped working, extended family on both sides, and a community of teammates and coaches who saw his potential and pushed it further.
What Comes Next

At twenty years old Alex Palmer is at the beginning of the next chapter. He has been accepted to multiple colleges and is expected to begin his studies soon — a milestone that represents not just his own achievement but the fulfilment of everything his family sacrificed to give him the chance to reach it.

He is working in the meantime — building, preparing, staying ready. The discipline that made him a cornerback on a varsity football team does not disappear when the season ends. It shows up in every room he walks into, every decision he makes, every goal he sets his sights on.

The journey from Portmore to the football fields of Florida is not a short one — geographically or emotionally. It required a grandmother who believed before anyone else did. A mother who sacrificed without complaint. A young man willing to adapt, to push, and to grow in unfamiliar soil. Alex Palmer did all three. And he is just getting started.

From the streets of Portmore to the varsity football field in Florida — Alex Palmer is proof that where you start does not determine where you finish. It just shapes how much you appreciate the journey.
body.cite: LWS Media Network

articles.title: Founders Talk EP3: The Truth About Entrepreneurship Nobody Tells You
articles.subtitle: The success stories are real. But so are the parts nobody talks about — the isolation, the self-doubt, the months where nothing works, and the version of yourself you have to become before the business becomes what you dreamed.
articles.author: Sasha Gaye Hemmings | LWS Media Network
articles.coverImageCaption: Founders Talk Episode 3 — Sasha Gaye Hemmings. Photo: LWS Media Network
articles.excerpt: The success stories are real. But so are the parts nobody talks about — the isolation, the self-doubt, the months where nothing works, and the version of yourself you have to become before the business becomes what you dreamed.

body.text: Welcome back to Founders Talk. I am Sasha Gaye Hemmings and today we are having a different kind of conversation. Over the past two weeks we talked about why people never start and what I wish I had known before launching my first business. Today I want to go somewhere even more honest. I want to talk about the things nobody tells you about entrepreneurship — the parts that get edited out of the success stories, the parts that almost broke me, and the parts that ultimately made me.

I want to say upfront — this is not a discouragement from building. If anything, I hope it is the opposite. Because the founders who make it are not the ones who never struggled. They are the ones who struggled and kept going anyway. But they deserve to know what they are getting into. You deserve to know what you are getting into.
Nobody Talks About the Loneliness

Entrepreneurship is one of the loneliest things I have ever done. Not because I did not have people around me — I did. But because the specific experience of building a business, carrying its weight, making decisions that affect your livelihood and potentially others, sitting with uncertainty at 2am — very few people in your life will truly understand that unless they have lived it themselves.

The people who love you will try. They will listen. They will encourage you. But there is a particular kind of isolation that comes with being the one who has to figure it out — who cannot fully off-load the burden because the business depends on you and only you. I learned to be more intentional about surrounding myself with other founders. People who do not need the experience explained. People who just get it.
Find your people. Not just people who support you — people who understand you. There is a difference. And in entrepreneurship, that difference is everything.
body.cite: Sasha Gaye Hemmings — Founders Talk

body.text: The Self-Doubt Never Fully Goes Away

I want to tell you that after a certain point — after enough clients, enough wins, enough evidence that you can do this — the self-doubt disappears. But that would not be true. What changes is your relationship with it. You learn to act despite it rather than waiting for it to leave. You learn to recognise it as fear, not as fact. You learn that the voice that says you are not enough is not a reliable narrator.

I have multiple degrees. I have helped over 134 clients build successful businesses. I have published books. I have built multiple companies simultaneously as a solo founder. And I still have moments of doubt. Still have days where I question whether I am doing enough, building fast enough, thinking big enough. The difference now is I do not let those moments make my decisions. I feel them, acknowledge them, and keep moving.
There Will Be Months Where Nothing Works

This is perhaps the most important thing I can tell any aspiring entrepreneur. There will be months — maybe several in a row — where despite your best efforts, your hardest work, and your most strategic thinking, the results simply do not come. Clients do not convert. Revenue stalls. Something you were counting on falls through. The plan you were executing stops working.

These months are not evidence that you are failing. They are part of the process. Every business I have ever studied — and I have studied many — has these seasons. What separates the businesses that survive them from the ones that do not is rarely strategy or talent. It is usually resilience. The ability to stay in motion even when the motion does not yet feel like progress.

I grew up learning resilience the hard way long before I started a business. The conditions of my childhood in Jamaica demanded it. In a strange way that background — the hardship, the years of navigating scarcity and uncertainty — prepared me for entrepreneurship better than any business course could have. When you have already survived hard things, the hard seasons in business become more manageable. Not easy. But survivable.
People Will Not Always Believe in You — And That Is Not the Problem

Some of the people closest to you will not understand what you are building. Some will question it openly. Some will offer advice disguised as concern that is really just their own fear being projected onto your dream. Some will wait quietly to see if you fail before deciding whether to support you.

This used to hurt me more than it does now. What I have come to understand is that other people's inability to see your vision is not a reflection of the vision — it is a reflection of their own limitations. Not everyone has the capacity to imagine something that does not yet exist. That is not a character flaw. It is just a human limitation. Your job is not to convince them. Your job is to build the thing and let the results speak.
The Business Will Demand You Become Someone New

This is perhaps the most profound truth about entrepreneurship that nobody prepares you for. The business you are trying to build requires a version of you that does not yet fully exist. You will need to develop confidence you do not currently have. You will need to learn skills that are currently outside your comfort zone. You will need to make decisions that terrify you and then live with the consequences either way.

Entrepreneurship is the most accelerated personal development programme on the planet. It will expose every limitation, every fear, every blind spot you have — and it will demand that you address them if you want to grow. The business does not just ask for your time and your talent. It asks for your full self. The version of you that shows up on day one of your business is rarely the version of you that is capable of running the business you are trying to build. The journey between those two versions is the real work.
You are not just building a business. You are building yourself. And sometimes — honestly, often — that is the harder and more important project of the two.
body.cite: Sasha Gaye Hemmings — Founders Talk

body.text: And Yet — It Is Worth It

After everything I have described — the loneliness, the doubt, the slow seasons, the people who did not believe, the constant demand to grow into someone bigger than you currently are — I want to be absolutely clear: I would do it all again. Without hesitation.

Because on the other side of all of that is something that employment can never give you. It is the ownership of your own time, your own decisions, your own direction. It is the ability to build something that reflects your values and serves the people you actually want to serve. It is watching an idea that lived only in your mind become something real that impacts real people. That feeling — that particular combination of terror and pride and purpose — is unlike anything else I have ever experienced.

I built Creative Minds Movement Services from nothing and helped over 134 clients do the same. I built Learning With Samara as a solo founder from the ground up. I built LWS Media Network — this platform — from an idea to a fully functioning global media company. I did all of this while raising children, writing books, and teaching students. Not because it was easy. Because it was mine.

That is the truth about entrepreneurship that nobody tells you loudly enough. Yes it is hard. Yes it will test you in ways you cannot currently anticipate. And yes — for the right person, with the right commitment — it is the most powerful and fulfilling thing you will ever do.

Thank you for being here for Founders Talk. Every week I will be in this space giving you the real conversation. No filters. No highlight reel. Just truth, insight, and the genuine desire to see you build something remarkable. See you next week.

articles.title: Founders Talk EP2: What I Wish I Knew Before Starting My First Business in 2018
articles.subtitle: If I could sit down with myself on the day I registered Creative Minds Movement Services and give her one hour of honest advice — this is exactly what I would say.
articles.author: Sasha Gaye Hemmings | LWS Media Network
articles.coverImageCaption: Founders Talk Episode 2 — Sasha Gaye Hemmings. Photo: LWS Media Network
articles.excerpt: If I could sit down with myself on the day I registered Creative Minds Movement Services and give her one hour of honest advice — this is exactly what I would say. No sugar coating. No highlight reel. Just the truth.

body.text: Welcome back to Founders Talk. I am Sasha Gaye Hemmings and this is the weekly space where I give you real, honest, no-fluff business insight from someone who has been building in the trenches since 2018. Last week we talked about why most people never start. This week I want to go deeper — and more personal. I want to talk about what I actually wish I had known before I launched my first business.

When I started Creative Minds Movement Services in 2018 I had degrees. I had knowledge. I had passion and drive and a genuine belief that I could build something meaningful. What I did not have was the full picture of what entrepreneurship actually looks like from the inside. There are things business school teaches you and there are things life teaches you. The second category is far more expensive and far more valuable.
1. Your Network Is Your Net Worth — Build It Before You Need It

I learned this the hard way. When you need clients, when you need collaborators, when you need someone to vouch for you — that is not the time to start building relationships. That time is before. Relationships built out of desperation feel like desperation. Relationships built over time, with genuine interest and reciprocity, become the foundation of a sustainable business.

I wish I had invested more time early on in showing up for other people — attending events, connecting with peers in my field, offering value before I needed anything in return. The clients I have retained longest, the partnerships that have meant the most — almost all of them came through relationships that were built quietly, without any immediate agenda.
2. Pricing Yourself Correctly Is an Act of Self-Respect

This one is painful to admit but I am going to say it anyway because I know I am not alone in this. When I started, I underpriced my services. Not because I did not know my value — but because I was afraid. Afraid clients would say no. Afraid I was not established enough to charge what my expertise was actually worth. That fear cost me time, energy, and money.

Here is what I know now: the right clients do not run from your price. The wrong clients always will. When you underprice yourself you attract people who do not value what you offer. When you price correctly you attract people who are serious, committed, and respectful of your work. Your price is a filter. Use it intentionally.
Undercharging is not humility. It is self-sabotage dressed up as accessibility. Know your worth. Charge accordingly. Apologise to no one.
body.cite: Sasha Gaye Hemmings — Founders Talk

body.text: 3. Systems Save Businesses. Passion Starts Them.

Passion will get you out of bed at 5am to work on your business. Passion will push you through the hard days. But passion alone will not keep a business running. What keeps a business running is systems — repeatable processes for onboarding clients, delivering services, following up, invoicing, managing time, and tracking results.

I spent too long running everything from my head. Every process lived in my memory rather than in a documented system. That works when you are small and everything is manageable. It breaks down the moment volume increases or you need someone else to step in. Build your systems early. Document your processes. Treat your business like it is going to grow — because if you do the work right, it will.
4. Not Every Client Is the Right Client

This took me longer to learn than I would like to admit. In the early days I said yes to almost everyone because I needed the revenue and I genuinely wanted to help. But not every client respects your boundaries, values your expertise, or operates in a way that is aligned with how you work. Some clients cost you more — in time, energy, and peace of mind — than they pay you.

Learning to qualify clients before committing — to ask the right questions, to notice the early warning signs, and to say no when a fit is not right — was one of the most transformative things I did for my business. The client list I am most proud of is not the longest one I have ever had. It is the one built on alignment, mutual respect, and genuine results.
5. Rest Is Part of the Strategy

Entrepreneurship culture celebrates hustle. It glorifies the grind. It treats rest like a reward you have not yet earned. I bought into that narrative for longer than I should have and it cost me. Burnout is real. It does not announce itself politely — it arrives quietly and then all at once, taking your creativity, your clarity, and your energy with it.

I am a mother, an educator, a founder, a consultant, an author, and a media publisher simultaneously. I have to be intentional about rest in a way that the hustle culture content I consumed early in my journey never taught me. Rest is not the absence of productivity. It is the prerequisite for it. Your best ideas, your clearest decisions, and your most powerful work come from a rested mind.
6. Your Story Is an Asset — Use It

I grew up with very little. My journey to where I am today was not smooth or linear or handed to me. For a long time I was hesitant to talk about that publicly. I worried it would make me seem less credible, less polished, less like someone people should trust with their business.

I was wrong. Your story is not a liability. It is your most powerful differentiator. There is no marketing campaign more compelling than a true account of someone who came from difficult circumstances and built something real. People do not just buy your service — they buy your story, your conviction, and their belief that if you could do it, maybe they can too.
I wish I had known sooner that the very things I tried to hide about my journey were the same things that would one day make people trust me most.
body.cite: Sasha Gaye Hemmings — Founders Talk

body.text: The Bottom Line

If I could go back to 2018 and sit with the version of myself about to start her first business, I would tell her this: the road is harder than you think and more rewarding than you can currently imagine. Price yourself right from the beginning. Build real relationships before you need them. Document your processes. Say no to the wrong clients so you have capacity for the right ones. Rest without guilt. And for the love of everything — tell your story. All of it. Because it is the most powerful thing you have.

Next week on Founders Talk we are getting into the truth about entrepreneurship that nobody tells you — the parts that the success stories leave out and the parts that almost broke me before they made me stronger. You do not want to miss it. See you then.

articles.title: Founders Talk EP1: Why Most People Never Start — And What To Do About It
articles.subtitle: Every week I sit down and talk business — real, honest, no-fluff conversations about entrepreneurship, building, and the mindset it takes to create something from nothing. This is Episode 1.
articles.author: Sasha Gaye Hemmings | LWS Media Network
articles.coverImageCaption: Founders Talk — Weekly business insights from Sasha Gaye Hemmings. Photo: LWS Media Network
articles.excerpt: Most people who want to start a business never do. Not because they lack talent. Not because they lack ideas. But because of something far more invisible and far more powerful — fear dressed up as practicality.

body.text: Welcome to Founders Talk — a weekly segment here on LWS Media Network where I sit down and talk business. Real conversations. No fluff. No curated highlight reel. Just honest, practical insight from someone who has been in the trenches of entrepreneurship since 2018, built businesses from the ground up, helped over 134 clients do the same, and learned — sometimes the hard way — what it actually takes to build something that lasts.

I am Sasha Gaye Hemmings. Founder. Educator. Consultant. Author. And every week in this space I am going to give you something useful. Something you can take away and apply. This is Episode 1 — and we are starting with the question I get asked most often, in one form or another, by almost everyone who comes to me wanting to build something of their own.
The Question Nobody Wants to Ask Out Loud

Why do most people never start? It is the elephant in the room of every entrepreneurship conversation. We talk about business plans, funding, marketing strategies, branding — all of it useful, all of it necessary. But none of it matters if you never actually begin. And the uncomfortable truth is that most people who say they want to start a business never do.

I have sat across from hundreds of aspiring entrepreneurs over the years. Talented people. Intelligent people. People with genuinely good ideas and real potential. And the single biggest thing that separates the ones who build something from the ones who do not is not money. It is not connections. It is not the right moment or the right circumstances. It is the decision to start despite not feeling ready.

Nobody feels ready. Readiness is not a feeling — it is a decision. The people who build things are not the ones who waited until they felt confident. They are the ones who moved while they were still afraid.
body.cite: Sasha Gaye Hemmings — Founders Talk

body.text: Fear Dressed Up as Practicality

Here is what I have learned: most people do not say they are afraid. They say they are being practical. They say they are waiting for the right time. They say they need more money, more experience, more research, more certainty. And all of those things sound reasonable. They are not unreasonable thoughts. But in most cases — not all, but most — they are fear dressed up in practical clothing.

Fear of failure. Fear of judgement. Fear of investing everything and losing it. Fear of what people will say if it does not work out. Fear of discovering that the idea they have been holding onto — the one that feels like it could be something — might not be as good as they hoped. These are real fears. I have felt all of them personally. I still feel some of them. The difference is I stopped letting them make my decisions for me.
The Myth of the Perfect Moment

One of the most damaging ideas in entrepreneurship is the idea that there is a perfect moment to start. There is not. There has never been. There will never be. Life does not pause to give you a clear runway. The bills do not stop while you get ready. The responsibilities do not disappear. The uncertainty does not resolve itself before you take the first step.

I started Creative Minds Movement Services in 2018. Was it the perfect moment? No. I faced real obstacles. I did not have everything figured out. What I had was a decision — a commitment to myself that I was going to do this. That I was going to show up even when it was uncomfortable, even when I was uncertain, even when the path was not clear. The clarity came from moving. Not from waiting.
What You Actually Need to Start

You need an idea that solves a real problem for real people. You need enough knowledge to begin — not to finish, just to begin. You need a willingness to learn what you do not yet know. And you need the courage to be imperfect in public while you figure it out. That is it. Everything else — the logo, the website, the business plan, the office — those come later. They are not prerequisites. They are the things you build as you go.

The entrepreneurs I have watched build the most remarkable things did not wait until they had all the answers. They started with a question — how can I solve this problem? — and they kept asking it every single day until a business formed around the answer. That is the process. It is messy and nonlinear and nothing like what they teach in business school. But it is real.
A Word to Anyone Sitting on an Idea Right Now

If you are reading this and you have an idea you have been sitting on — weeks, months, maybe years — I want to speak directly to you. The fact that the idea is still there means something. Ideas that are not meant for you do not stick around. They fade. But the ones that keep coming back, the ones that wake you up at night, the ones you think about in quiet moments — those are worth taking seriously.

You do not have to quit your job tomorrow. You do not have to have the funding or the perfect plan. But you do have to do something. Write it down. Tell one trusted person. Register the business name. Buy the domain. Do one small concrete thing that makes it real. Because the moment it becomes real — even slightly, even imperfectly — it stops being a dream and starts being a business.
The world does not need more people with good ideas. It needs more people willing to do something with them. Start imperfectly. Start scared. Just start.
